E:\\videos\\mickey6\\wt\\vlog\\mickey6\\.text: See this pork shoulder? I just pulled it apart with two fingers. No fork, no knife. Eight hours ago, this was the toughest, cheapest piece of meat in my whole case. And most people ruin it for one reason. They rush it. A fella came in here last month, a bus driver, nice man. He paid $24 for one pound of pulled pork at a barbecue place downtown. And he said, Mickey, I want to make this at home. So he bought a shoulder from me, took it home and cooked it at 400 degrees for three hours because the recipe on his phone said so. He came back on Monday with a piece of it wrapped in foil. He put it on my counter and said, look at this. It was gray, dry on the outside, chewy in the middle. And when he tried to pull it apart, it just tore into hard little strings. He said, I followed the recipe, Mickey. What did I do wrong? Maybe that's your pork too.

You wanted that soft, juicy, falls-apart pork you get at a good barbecue place, and you got a hard roast you had to chew like gum. It was never you. It was the clock. Somebody told you a pork shoulder could be done fast, and nobody behind a meat counter ever told you why it can't. So here's my promise. By the end of this video, you'll make a pork shoulder so tender, It falls apart when you look at it for about $16 and it'll feed your family three nights. Seven old Irish butcher tricks. Nothing fancy to buy, no smoker, no gadgets. And trick number five is going to sound crazy. When the meat stops cooking, you leave it alone. Stay with me for that one. If you're new here, I'm Mickey, Mickey Callahan. I've been cutting meat in this narrow little shop in Dorchester, Boston since 1972 and my father before me. 54 years at this block.

My mother was from County Cork, and every Sunday of my life, there was a pork shoulder in her oven before we left for church. It was ready when we came home. That was the whole secret. Time. Trick number one is buying the right piece, because half the people who ruin a pork shoulder ruin it right here at the meat case. There are two pieces with the word shoulder on the label, and they are not the same. The top half of the shoulder is called the Boston Butt. Funny name, I know. It's not the back end of the pig at all. It's the upper shoulder. Back in the old days, here in Boston, butchers packed these cuts in barrels. And a barrel was called a butt. So Boston Butt, that's the one you want. the bottom half is called the picnic it's got the skin on it's leaner and it's got more tough muscle around the leg

It's cheaper by maybe 20 cents a pound, and it's a good piece of meat, but it's harder to get right. If you're new at this, buy the butt, and buy it with the bone in. Look for a piece about 7 or 8 pounds, with a flat bone showing on one side. That's the blade bone. The bone holds heat in the middle of the meat. It keeps the meat from drying out, and later, it's going to tell you exactly when the pork is done. A boneless roast all tied up in a net looks neater but it cooks drier every time. Look at the color too. You want a deep pink almost red with white fat running all through it like marble. Pale meat with no fat inside is going to come out dry no matter what you do. In my shop a bone-in butt runs about $2 a pound. 8 pounds, $16. That's the cheapest dinner in the building. Trick number two, leave the fat on.

Everybody wants to trim it all off because fat is bad and they stand there at the counter cutting off the white cap on top. Don't do that. That fat cap is your basting. For eight hours it melts slowly down over the meat and keeps the outside from drying out. What you do instead is score it. Take a sharp knife and cut a crosshatch pattern into the fat about an inch apart like a tic-tac-toe board. Cut through the fat but not into the meat. A quarter inch deep is plenty. That lets the salt get in and it lets the fat render out slowly instead of sliding off in one sheet. If the fat cap is very thick, more than an inch, you can trim it down to about a quarter inch. only the top. Leave all the fat inside the meat alone. That's the fat that makes it juicy. And any skin, if you bought a picnic, take the skin off or score it deep. Skin never gets soft in a dry oven. Trick number three.

Salt it the night before. Here's what actually happens. Salt on the surface pulls a little juice out of the meat. Then, over the next few hours, that salty juice goes back in, deep into the meat, and it changes the meat so it holds on to its own juice when you cook it. Salt it right before the oven and it only seasons the outside. The measure is simple. One teaspoon of kosher salt for every pound of meat. Eight pounds, eight teaspoons. Mix it with two tablespoons of brown sugar and a spoon of black pepper and rub it all over into the cuts in the fat into every corner around the bone. Then put it on a plate in the refrigerator uncovered. No plastic wrap. The cold air dries the outside a little and a dry outside is what gives you that dark sticky crust later. Leave it there overnight. 12 hours is good. 24 is better.

My mother salted hers on Saturday night every week and she never once owned a thermometer. Trick number four, low heat. This is the big one and this is where that bus driver went wrong. 400 degrees is for chicken. A pork shoulder wants 275. That's it. 275 degrees for a long time. Here's why. A shoulder is a muscle the pig used every single day walking around. It's full of tough connective tissue, collagen, and collagen only melts slowly at low heat over hours. When it melts it turns into gelatin and gelatin is what makes pulled pork soft and silky. You can't hurry it. It takes the time it takes. When you blast the oven, the outside of the meat squeezes tight like a fist, and it pushes all the juice out before the collagen inside even starts to melt. So you get the worst of both. Dry on the outside, tough on the inside.

That's exactly what was in his foil. So take the shoulder out of the refrigerator an hour before. Set the oven to 275. Put the meat fat side up in a heavy roasting pan, on a rack if you have one, or on a bed of thick sliced onions if you don't. Count on about an hour and a half for every pound. An eight pound shoulder, about 10-11 hours. put it in the oven before bed or first thing in the morning and go live your day and here's the old irish part pour one bottle of dark stout into the bottom of the pan not over the meat into the pan a cup of apple cider works too or plain water if that's what you have that liquid keeps the drippings from burning and the steam keeps the oven moist and at the end those drippings are gold. Trick number five, the one that sounds crazy. Somewhere around the middle of the cook, the meat is going to stop cooking.

You'll check the thermometer at 160 degrees and an hour later it's still at 160. Two hours later, maybe 165. And everybody panics. They turn the oven up to 400 and that's how they ruin it. Here's what actually happens. That's called the stall. The meat is sweating. The juice comes to the surface and cools it off. the same way you cool off when you sweat. And at the same time, inside, that collagen is finally melting. That's the most important part of the whole cook. The stall is not a problem. The stall is the meat getting tender. So you leave it alone. Don't open the door every half hour. Every time you open the door, you lose about 20 minutes. If you need to speed it up a little, there's one old trick.

Once the outside is dark and firm, wrap the shoulder tight in foil or butcher paper with a few spoons of the pan juice inside. It pushes it through the stall faster and keeps every drop of juice in the package. That's all. Wrap it, don't crank it. Trick number six, forget the clock. The pork is done when the pork says it's done, and there are two ways it tells you. The first one is the number. Push a thermometer into the thickest part, away from the bone. You want 200 to 205 degrees. I know, the store sticker says pork is safe at 145, and that's true. It's safe, and it's sliceable, but it's not pulled pork. At 170, it's still tight. Somewhere past 195, the meat lets go. That's the number where collagen is gone and gelatin is everywhere. The second way is the one my father taught me and it never lies.

Grab that blade bone with a towel and give it a little wiggle. If it's done, the bone moves like a loose tooth and it slides out clean without a single piece of meat on it. If the bone fights you, it's not ready. Close the oven another hour and try again. And one more test. Poke the meat with a thermometer or a fork. It should go in like butter, no push at all. If you have to push, it's not done. Every shoulder is different. One might be done in nine hours, the next one in eleven. That's why you never trust the clock. Trick number seven, rest it and rest it long. This is the one everybody skips because the house smells so good and everybody's standing in the kitchen with a plate. You pull it out of the oven and you start tearing it apart with two forks right there. and all that juice runs out onto the board and dries up in the air. Here's the old way.

Leave it wrapped in the foil. Wrap a couple of old bath towels around it and put the whole thing in an empty picnic cooler and close the lid. Leave it there one hour. Two is fine. It'll stay hot for four. While it rests, the juice that was pushed to the outside goes back into the meat and the gelatin thickens up. Then you pull it. Put on a pair of rubber gloves or use two forks. and pull it apart into big pieces, not little threads. Pick out the bone and the soft fat you don't want. Then take those pan drippings, skim the fat off the top, and pour about a cup back over the meat. Toss it with your hands. Every piece shines. That's the pork that falls apart. That's what $24 a pound downtown tastes like. Now, if something went wrong, here's what it means. If the pork is tough and won't pull, it's not overcooked, it's undercooked That's the one everybody gets backwards

Tough means the collagen isn't done melting. Put it back wrapped another hour or two. If it pulls apart but it's dry and stringy, it was cooked too hot, or it didn't rest, or you bought a lean boneless piece with no fat inside. Tonight, the pan juice is your fix. Pour it on and toss it, and it'll come back. Next time, bone in, fat on, 275. If it's soft but mushy, like baby food, it was swimming. You covered it in liquid in a slow cooker for 10 hours. That's boiled pork, not roasted pork. Next time, the liquid stays in the bottom of the pan, under the meat, and if it tastes flat, it's salt. A pinch over the pulled meat, toss it, taste again. My mother never wrote any of this down. she'd salt it on Saturday put it in the oven at 7 on Sunday morning before Mass and she'd tell me don't you dare open that door

I was eight years old, and I wanted to open that door more than anything in the world. We'd come home at noon, and the whole street smelled like it. She'd pull out that bone with her bare fingers, clean as a whistle, and she'd hand it to my father like a trophy. Sixty years later, I still check every shoulder the same way. If the bone comes out clean, my mother would have approved. Now let's do the money because this is the best deal in the whole meat case. One bone in Boston butt, 8 pounds, at about $2 a pound is $16. After the bone and the fat cook off, you've got about 5 pounds of pulled pork. That's a little over $3 a pound. That pulled pork downtown was $24 a pound. Five pounds of it is $120. You made the same thing for 16, plus a bottle of stout and some salt. Nobody's a villain here.

They pay rent. They pay cooks. It's just arithmetic. And that one shoulder is three nights of dinner. Sunday, pulled pork on soft rolls with a little of the juice. Tuesday, pork tacos, crisp in a hot pan. Thursday, my favorite, a pork hash with potatoes and an egg on top. Freeze the rest in its own juice, in flat bags, and it tastes the same in a month. So let's go over it once. Buy the Boston butt, bone in, about 8 pounds, with fat all through it. Score the fat cap, don't cut it off. Salt it the night before, 1 teaspoon a pound, uncovered in the fridge. 275 degrees with a bottle of stout in the pan when it stalls leave it alone or wrap it it's done at 200 when the bone slides out clean and rest it an hour in a cooler before you pull it your homework is simple

Next time, buy the bone-in butt and set the oven to 275 instead of 400. Only those two things. That's all it takes to never rush a pork shoulder again. And tell me in the comments, what did your family put in the bottom of the pan? Beer, cider, coffee, something nobody else did? And where are you watching from? I read every one of them right here at the counter between customers. Next time I'm going to show you how a $5 chuck roast can eat like a ribeye with one old butcher trick most people have never heard of. You'll never pay steakhouse prices again. Until then my friend leave that oven door shut.
